look_here_first: Start with the bark: mature trunks and limbs shed thin outer layers to expose smooth cream, pink, apricot, orange, or red inner bark. Then confirm evergreen simple leaves, urn-shaped pale flowers, and orange-to-red berry-like fruit.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: distinctive exfoliating bark revealing smooth pale cream, pink, apricot, orange, or red inner bark

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: clusters of pale urn- to bell-shaped flowers

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Ericaceae-style anthers opening by apical pores

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: round fleshy berry-like fruit ripening from green through orange to red

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Hill Country/West Texas rocky woodland and canyon association

key_traits.label: Bark
key_traits.text: The peeling, multicolored smooth bark is the fastest whole-plant recognition cue in mature Texas madrone.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Pale fused urceolate/campanulate flowers occur in clusters; inspect the stamens for the characteristic Ericaceae poricidal-anther pattern.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: Round fleshy fruits mature through orange/red and are eaten/dispersed by birds.

key_traits.label: Ecology
key_traits.text: Occurs naturally in rocky or canyon woodland settings; establishment can be associated with nurse-tree shade on the Edwards Plateau.
